newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Sri Lanka develops tea cola for market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sri Lanka develops tea cola for market.

text.p: Scientists at Sri Lanka's Tea Research Institute (TRI) are developing new products for the ready-to-drink tea market dominated by the likes of beverage giants Coca-Cola and PepsiCo.
"Sri Lanka is being left behind in the scramble to cater for the tastes of a new generation looking for convenient health beverages," said TRI director Wester Modder.

"Traditionally, we have been exporting bulk tea to Western markets," he told Reuters in an interview. "If we make the value-addition here, we'll have an instant take off. This is where the market is."

The Indian Ocean island will need to ship 260 million kg of tea by 2005 to maintain its 18-20 percent share of the global market, and must diversify its products and add value while winning back traditional markets, Modder said.
The TRI, nestled in the lush green tea estates of the central hills, pioneered research into value-added teas and needs its work to be taken up by entrepreneurs.
Modder said TRI patented an instant tea product in the 1960s but could not market it because the institute did not have the means to do so and local companies lacked financial muscle.
Senior research officer Anudini Liyanage said a liquid tea concentrate perfected by the TRI's biochemistry division was now available for commercial exploitation.
The concentrate, precursor for the preparation of carbonated tea, comes with a range of flavours like apple, pineapple and strawberry, she said.
TEA PATENT FOR SALE -- ON CONDITION
The patent is offered for sale on the condition that only Sri Lankan tea is used in making the tea concentrate and that the plant be located on the island.

Plantations Industry Ministry officials said the industry should learn from the way Coca-Cola and PepsiCo, which both have ready-to-drink teas, aggressively pitch their products to young people around the world.

The director-general of the Sri Lanka Tea Board, Ranjith Maligaspe, has said tea needs to discard its staid image and use the sort of snappy marketing techniques that make soft drinks attractive to younger consumers.
He told an Asia Tea Industry conference in Singapore last year that it was vital to develop a new image and new markets for tea because global output was rising but demand was static.

Modder said TRI scientists were also researching the health benefits of tea drinking, hoping to promote tea as a health drink in the drive to capture a larger share of the multi-million dollar beverage market.
Current research, mostly on green tea, has shown it has properties that fight cancer and cardio-vascular diseases, he said. About 70-to-80 percent of world trade is in black tea.

Sri Lanka, the world's leading tea exporter, still exports most of its tea in bulk as it has done for more than a 100 years. But exporters are gradually realising the importance of selling value-added products, tea industry experts said.

Exports of Ceylon tea remain the island's main net foreign exchange earner. About half of its total tea export earnings of 24 billion rupees ($421 million) in 1995 came from value-added teas, the experts said.
Tea exports are expected to hit a record 250 million kg in 1996, from 245 million kg in the previous year.
